summary:
Abia is a state in southern Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 has been in force since January 2014 and applies across the country, to visitors as well as residents. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law, and that exposure begins at the point of entry into Abia.

The Act's reach extends well beyond sexual conduct. Entering a same-sex marriage or civil union is punishable by 14 years' imprisonment, and anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of such a union, or who supports the registration, operation or sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings, faces 10 years' imprisonment. Public displays of a same-sex amorous relationship are also punishable.

Sharia penal codes do not apply in Abia. The twelve northern states operating sharia criminal law for Muslims are Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara; Abia is not among them, so the death-penalty exposure reported under sharia provisions in those states does not reach this southern state. The federal penalties and the national arrest climate, however, apply in full.

The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note records tens of LGBT+ arrests per year in Nigeria, alongside police harassment including beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. At least four sharia death sentences have been imposed since 2022, none carried out.

A 2022 federal court ruling struck down sections of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act as unconstitutional; the scope of the provisions that remain in force is not specified in the source.
tangentialFactors:
The national enforcement pattern documented elsewhere in Nigeria includes mass arrests at social venues, which sets the ambient risk level for any gathering a visitor might attend in Abia. Police forces in southern states have used the Act against people for appearance rather than conduct, as in a documented Lagos case where a man was stopped and assaulted for 'looking gay'.

Dating applications carry documented entrapment risk nationally, with 'kito' gangs luring LGBTQ+ Nigerians through apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. This risk is not Abia-specific but reaches any visitor using such apps in the state.
localsOnly:
Residents of Abia live under the federal 14-year framework and the national climate of arrests and community hostility, without the sharia layer that applies to Muslims in northern states. Activists report that the Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work; many fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to police.

A 2022 federal court ruling struck down sections of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act as unconstitutional, though the source does not specify which sections remain in force.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Abia-specific enforcement incidents, arrests, prosecutions or local police practice; the enforcement picture is drawn from national and other-state reporting and is unresolved as to Abia itself.

The scope of the provisions struck down by the 2022 federal court ruling is not specified in the sources and remains unresolved.

No Abia-specific data on document markers, facilities access, or care availability for trans residents was identified in the inventory.
